body:
@domenic some thoughts following our chat:

Right now, history entries are keyed by step number, 0, 1, 2, 3… meaning the navigable needs to go up to the top level to find out the next step number when it's creating a new entry. Instead, I'm going to key it by timestamp. This means a navigable can create a history entry on its own, then notify the top level. There'll be a little bit of conflict resolution here, in case the top level has already advanced to a later timestamp.

Once the top level is notified about a change in history position, it checks to see if any other navigables need to change history entry as a result.

However, I think I still need the above algorithm to look up `history.length`.

That caters for adding a history entry synchronously, but how important is it that `appHistory` can traverse to a _previous_ history entry synchronously? As far as I can tell, this is a new capability. `back()` and `forward()` appear to be async, even if it goes to an entry that was added synchronously.

body:
So, this kind of is related to how I wasn't sure I clearly communicated yesterday, and am not sure I was pushing you in the right direction.

Indeed, appHistory as currently specced doesn't perform synchronous traversal itself. It currently does all navigations async. It even imagines existing synchronous navigations becoming async, but see https://github.com/WICG/app-history/issues/19 for how that seems unrealistic.

Thus, my main concern is same-document synchronous traversals that are performed with existing APIs. E.g., `history.back()`, `location.hash = ...`, `history.pushState()`, etc. It would be ideal if appHistory could see such changes, and reflect them into `appHistory.entries`, synchronously. So my main concern is about getting a synchronous view, not performing a synchronous traversal.

Additionally, one route for solving https://github.com/WICG/app-history/issues/19 would be that same-document navigation "in some sense" (e.g. updating `location.href`) is alway sync, while in another sense it completes asynchronously. This is messy and not something I prefer, but I'd kind of like to keep the options open since that issue is so hard. This would probably require ("in some sense") synchronous traversal, but I'm not sure how that impacts your work here. Like, maybe it could seem synchronous to `appHistory.entries`, `location.href`, etc., but `history.length` and other frames' views of history only get updated asynchronously?

My other, more abstract confusion was, if "new APIs must not synchronously queue session history traversal steps", what must they do instead? And how is that new thing better? It seems like `history.length` is going to be screwy either way. It's a bit hard to understand because nothing is using either "synchronously queue session history traversal steps" or anything similar to it (e.g., you haven't updated the `history.back()` steps), so I'm not sure what the world will look like.

body:
Thanks for the clarification. From my testing it seems that we only ever traverse synchronously to new session history entries created by hash changes and `pushState`. `back()`/`forward()`/`go()` appear to be async.

So, feel free to allow `appHistory` to synchronously create new entries like `pushState` does, but I'll leave that up to you. Accessing entries in a sync way is no problem at all.

I think this will all work out fine.

Right now navigables have a map of history step number to history entry. I'm going to change this to be just a list of history entries. The step number will be moved to the history entry. This means a navigable can synchronously create and traverse to a new history entry, which will have a step of -1 as a placeholder. Then, asynchronously, the history entry will be given the correct step number.

I'm going to keep "synchronously queue session history traversal steps" around for now, but I think it's only `history.length` that needs it. If that's the case I'll just inline it.

body:
Moving this bullet up slightly changed the semantics and gives the user agent less freedom than they had before. Previously the user agent "may" show the prompt, and the annoying/deceptive/pointless issue was something they could consider. Now they must show the prompt, unless it's annoying/deceptive/pointless.

I think it'd be better to retain the previous structure, with "may" covering everything in the "Then" clause you have.

body: (Answering these in a slightly different order because I think it makes more sense) > So there are four session history entries in that example, right? (One for each URL.) Yep! > Why are they stored so differently between traversables navigables vs. other navigables? > > I'm surprised that the spec infrastructure isn't more like the diagram, where (it appears) that each navigable has a list of session history entries, and it doesn't vary depending on top-level vs. not. That makes me feel less bad for sinking a load of time on a design exactly like that, but I later moved it all into the traversable. I might still be wrong, but here's my reasoning: Navigables can be created synchronously. Eg, creating an iframe. They can also be destroyed synchronously. Eg, removing an iframe. A history traversal needs to be somewhat atomic, which is why there's a single queue on the traversable. When the history data was spread across all the navigables, it look a massive amount of task queuing just to figure out which navigables were going to navigate for a single traversal. This opened it up to a lot of race conditions. A navigable's history also needs to outlive the navigable. Navigating to step 4 will destroy the iframe navigable (unless bfcache), but going back to step 3 will restore the `//hello` history entry into a new navigable in a new iframe in a new document. Either this data needs to be moved around when the navigable is destroyed/restored in an atomic way, or it could _always_ live somewhere else. I haven't spec'd the bit where new navigables are associated with old session history, but I want to prepare the model for that. The "somewhere else" model seemed simplest. It isn't race-free, as there'll be a period where an iframe navigable is created, but the traversable's history tree is unaware of it. Similarly, there'll be a period where the iframe is removed but the traversable still holds history state for it. In both cases tasks will be queued in the traversables session history queue to update the model, similar to how the history tree is modified when navigations are performed. These races seem ok, because they're very similar to the synchronous navigation races (hashchange/pushState) that the model already has to deal with. > Where are they stored? How many lists are involved, and how would you reach each of those lists from the top-level traversable? ``` Traversable ┣━ Session history traversal queue. A parallel queue, used to edit… ┗┓ Session history entries. A list, each has: ┗┓ Document state ┗┓ Nested histores. A list, each has: ┣━ ID (referencing a navigable's ID) ┗━ Session history entries. A list. Navigable ┗ ID. A unique ID. ``` A [traversable](https://whatpr.org/html/6315/history.html#traversable-navigable) has a list of [session history entries](https://whatpr.org/html/6315/history.html#tn-session-history-entries), which represent the top-level history items (`//app`, `//app#foo`, `//bar` in the above diagram). A [history entry](https://whatpr.org/html/6315/history.html#session-history-entry) has a [document state](https://whatpr.org/html/6315/history.html#she-document-state). This holds the document for the entry, but also state needed to recreate the document if the document is destroyed. A [document state](https://whatpr.org/html/6315/history.html#document-state) as [nested histories](https://whatpr.org/html/6315/history.html#document-state-nested-histories), which holds the session history entries for nested navigables in that document. A [nested history](https://whatpr.org/html/6315/history.html#nested-history) has an ID and a list of history entries. An ID is used rather than a reference to the navigable, so the state can be serialised. Eventually, other information will be added here to reassociate session history on traversal (like target name, position in DOM at parse time). "get session history entries" walks this tree to get the list for a particular navigable.

OK, that makes sense. I think the task-queuing could have been avoided if you'd stored things on the navigable for convenience/understandability, but said that they should only be accessed by the traversible. But the issue where an navigable's history needs to outlive the navigable clinches it in favor of storing things in a centralized location.

What remains for me to understand is why you chose the particular structure (as depicted in your Unicode-art diagram). In particular there is a lot of nesting, but I'm unsure which parts are essential versus incidental. Would it work to flatten things out as follows? Probably not, but I'd be interested to know why:

```
Traversable
┣━ Session history traversal queue. A parallel queue, used to edit…
┗┓ Session history entries. A list, each has:
 ┣━ Document state
 ┣━ ID (referencing a navigable's ID) 
 ┗━ Session history entries. A list.
```

Also, trying to figure out where the four session history entries from your diagram are located, I still get confused, mainly because I think of navigables as owning their own list of session history entries, so instead saying I have to traverse from traversible -> pick a session history entry -> document state -> nested histories -> pick a nested history -> session history entries -> find the nested session history entry is a lot.

Is it something like this?

```
Traversable's session history entries:
 - //app/
   - This session history entry's document state's nested histories:
      - 0
        - ID: iframe ID
        - session history entries:
          - //yo
 - //app/#foo
   - This session history entry's document state's nested histories:
      - 0
        - ID: iframe ID
        - session history entries:
          - //yo
      - 1
        - ID: iframe ID
        - session history entries:
          - //hello
```

I guess even with the necessity of things being centralized, I would have anticipated a structure where instead of traversing down all those levels, I could instead "read off the diagram". Every cell in your diagrams is identifiable by two "coordinates", the step and the navigable (ID). I would have expected us to be able to reflect that in the spec, i.e. by having the traversible hold the equivalent of the diagram somehow...

body:
Here is the simplest way I see to translate your diagrams into "computer science concepts" while still letting their nature shine through:

- Each traversible holds a map from navigable IDs (including the traversible itself) to lists of session history entries.
- Each session history entry has a step.

Then you can do operations like:

- To get all session history entries for a given navigable, just look it up in the map.
- To get all the session history entries for a given step, loop over each session history list and find the first that matches the step (or give up if you go past the step)
- To get all the steps, I guess traverse every session history entry list? Maybe there's something more efficient you could do.

body:
Thanks for all the explanations. I think this all makes sense now and I'm happy for you to proceed. The fact that the mapping between the diagrams and spec data structures is so involved is a bit unfortunate, but I guess worth the cost...

Still, let me keep digging at the relative complexity question a bit further.

> It makes that particular operation simpler, but it makes other operations more complicated.

This is only true because you've hidden the nested traversal inside "get session history entries". If you inlined that (which is, mentally, what I had to do while reading this PR) you'd see that the current version is quite complicated.

> Let redundantNavigables be the result of posting tasks into the document, and their descendant documents, to discover all the navigables that are about to be discarded.

This should not be necessary in my flattened model. All the data lives in the traversable; there's no need to post tasks (except sometimes a single task to go up to the level of the traversable).

So the delta comes in having to discover the navigables which a given operation has killed off, and then cleaning them. I can see how that's not as clean in some ways. But it's at least easy to map to the diagrams :).
